title: Love has teeth!
content:
The cedar handle of the charting brush creaked under the pressure of Kaya’s grip. She didn’t realize she was doing it until her knuckles flared stark white against the wood. Across the room, the faint, maddening sound of Julian humming a mindless tune scraped against her nerves like glass on stone. He had just ruined a second vellum scroll by spilling water across the ink-lines, and his immediate response had been a helpless, defensive shrug. “You know how clumsy I am with liquid measures, Kaya. You shouldn’t have left it on my bench.”

​A familiar, bitter heat surged from her chest to her jaw. Kaya clenched her teeth so hard her molars ached.

​I am surrounded by idiots.

​For months, that phrase had been her silent shield. It was the armor she put on every morning to survive the suffocating weight of her life. She had used it to rationalize her family’s careless disregard when they botched the coordinates she paid six figures for. She had used it to numb the pain when her Director blocked her promotion because she was “too intelligent to risk losing.” She had used it to endure her Elder Guardians’ soft, paralyzing lectures about staying safe on the shore.

​But as she stood there, watching Julian casually walk away from the mess he expected her to clean, the armor shattered.

​It wasn’t a shield anymore. It was a mirror.

​With a sudden, jarring clarity, Kaya realized the terrifying truth: the “pressured-love” she had been practicing was a lie. She had been taught that to be good, to be noble, to be a protector, meant keeping the peace. It meant smiling through the incompetence, absorbing the chaos of others, and quietly redrawing the maps they ruined so the guild wouldn’t collapse.

​It wasn’t virtue. It was a hostage situation. And she was the one volunteering to stay in the cell.

​The sheer weight of the others emotions she had been tolerating rushed over her. By pretending relationships were fine while the evil charade unfolded, she hadn’t been preserving peace—she had been funding her own slow, psychological death. She felt secure in her routine, yes, but she felt entirely, utterly dead.

​Her fist clenched tightly around the brush, the wood groaning a final warning before it snapped neatly in two.

​The sharp crack echoed through the silent drafting hall. Julian startled, turning around. “Kaya? What was that?”

​Kaya didn’t answer. She dropped the broken pieces of the brush onto the table. The heat in her chest suddenly cooled into something terrifyingly sharp, clinical, and absolute. The honest person inside her finally woke up: soulless conformity never leads to life-giving change.

​”I’m not cleaning it,” Kaya said, her voice dropping to a calm, dead pan.

​Julian blinked, confused. “What? But the ink will stain the cedar if it sets—”

​”Then let it stain,” she interrupted, stepping out from behind her desk. For the first time, she didn’t soften her posture. She didn’t sigh and reach for the cloth. She let the mess exist. She let his failure belong entirely to him.

​She walked past him without a glance, heading straight for the grand archive doors. She could feel the anchors pulling at her ankles—the thought of her disappointed parents, her patronizing Director, her suffocating guardians—but the ropes were fraying.

​To hate what is wrong meant she had to stop participating in the illusion. If they wanted to live in a world of self-inflicted chaos, they were welcome to it. But they would no longer use her as their safety net.

​Kaya reached into her pocket, her fingers brushing against the cold glass vial of her secret, un-spillable ink. She didn’t need to fight them. She didn’t need to argue, or scream, or demand they understand her worth. She just had to stop carrying them.

​She opened the heavy oak doors, stepping out into the bright, biting air of the city, leaving the midday work behind.

If she had to brave the wild tides to get the pearl, she would do it completely alone—and for the first time in years, her jaw was unlocked, her hands were open, and she could finally breathe.
